newsitem.title: USA: SEC urges exchanges to re-examine circuit breakers.
newsitem.headline: SEC urges exchanges to re-examine circuit breakers.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Thursday urged the nation's stock exchanges to re-examine market circuit breakers, which are intended to prevent a full-blown crisis in times of market volatility.

The SEC asked the exchanges to reach a consensus "as soon as possible on the size of increases in the current trigger levels required to ensure that cross market trading halts are imposed only during market declines of historic proportions."
The SEC issued the order as it approved applications by the American, New York and Philadelphia stock exchanges to extend circuit breakers for only six months.

Since 1988, when the SEC approved adoption of circuit breakers when the markets become overheated, the agency had routinely extended the so-called pilot programmes for a year, after they expired on Oct. 31. The circuit breakers were first adopted following the market crash in October 1987.
In allowing the extension, the SEC said six months will give the exchanges "more than sufficient time" to agree on proper trigger levels and procedures under prevailing market levels.

In its order Thursday, the SEC said it expected the exchanges to re-evaluate and adjust circuit breaker trigger levels promptly to prevent imposing cross-market trading halts that are not justified by the overall magnitude of a market decline.
It said it also expects the exchanges to submit their proposals for new trigger levels by Feb. 3, 1997. It also asked for public comment on the issue.
The SEC said it "continues to have significant concerns that the levels for triggering trading halts need to be increased to reflect the market rise since the breakers' inception."

The original circuit breaker rules, which were adopted on a pilot basis, called for trading to be halted for one hour if the Dow Jones industrial average declined 250 points from its previous day's closing level. Thereafter, trading would halt for an additional two hours if the Dow declined 400 points from the previous close.

In July of 1996, the SEC modified the time periods for trading halts so that if the Dow declined by 250 points, trading would stop for one-half hour and if it dropped further to a 400-point loss, trading would cease for one hour.

The SEC said although the revised trigger points have never been reached, "the commission believes that increases in circuit breaker trigger levels to reflect current market levels should be developed by the exchanges as soon as possible."
The SEC said that when it adopted those revisions, it already noted the need to increase trading halt trigger levels to prevent the unnecessary application of the breakers.
It added that the continued rise in the Dow since July further reinforces its concerns.

The agency said that at current market levels, the 250- and the 400-point triggers represent declines of only 4.1 percent and 6.6 percent, respectively. When adopted in 1988, the trigger points reflected one-day declines of 12 percent and 19 percent.
"The Commission has serious doubts whether a 4.1 percent decline warrants a market-wide halt," the SEC said.

It said the 1988 threshold has been reached only once since 1945 -- during the "Black Monday" crash on Oct. 19, 1987, when the Dow plunged 508 points, or 22.63 percent. In comparison, the current 4.1 percent threshold for the first trading halt has been reached 13 separate occasions since 1945, it said.
